description: Richard's resignation, Monck's march south and the return of Charles II — how the republic ended.
content_html:
The Collapse of the Republic 1658–1660

Oliver Cromwell had held the republic together through personal authority and military reputation. When he died in September 1658, no comparable figure existed. His son Richard Cromwell had no military career, no independent power base, and commanded little respect in the army. When he summoned Parliament in 1659, MPs challenged the army’s political role. The army responded by forcing Richard to dissolve Parliament. Then, under sustained pressure from army grandees, Richard resigned in May 1659 after only eight months as Lord Protector — derisively nicknamed “Tumbledown Dick” by contemporaries.

After Richard’s resignation England entered a period of rapid constitutional instability. The Rump Parliament was recalled, dissolved again, and recalled a second time. Army factions jostled for control. The country was exhausted by a decade of military government, heavy taxation, and moral policing. A restoration of monarchy was beginning to seem, to many, the only path to stable, legitimate government.

Key Fact

Richard Cromwell resigned in May 1659 after only eight months as Lord Protector. He lacked military authority and was forced out by army officers. England then entered months of constitutional chaos before George Monck intervened.

George Monck and the March South

George Monck commanded the English army in Scotland — a well-paid, disciplined force that had not participated in the political intrigues of the English army. In January 1660, Monck marched south with his army, moving deliberately towards London. His intentions were opaque: he spoke of restoring constitutional government but did not declare openly for the King. His presence stabilised an increasingly chaotic situation. He arrived in London in February 1660.

Monck’s critical act was ordering the readmission of the members excluded by Pride’s Purge in 1648 — the Presbyterian MPs who had opposed the regicide. This reconstituted the Long Parliament in something like its original form. On 16 March 1660 this revived Parliament dissolved itself, calling for elections to a new “Convention Parliament.”

Before the Convention Parliament met, Charles II issued the Declaration of Breda (April 1660), setting out the terms on which he would return. It made four key promises: a general pardon for all except those Parliament excluded; liberty of conscience in religion; settlement of the army’s back pay; and resolution of disputed land ownership through parliamentary statute. Crucially, all four were referred to Parliament for final decision. Charles was not making unconditional promises but was deferring to parliamentary authority — a deliberately reassuring constitutional signal. In practice, all four promises were partially walked back after the Restoration.

The Restoration: May 1660

The Convention Parliament met in April 1660 and voted to restore the monarchy. Charles II returned to England in May 1660, entering London on 29 May to popular celebration. The Indemnity and Oblivion Act (1660) offered pardon to most who had participated in the republic, with notable exceptions including the “regicides” — the men who had signed Charles I’s death warrant. Thirteen were executed; others were imprisoned or went into exile.

The constitutional terms of the Restoration were deliberately left ambiguous. Charles II returned as king with broadly the powers his father had possessed before 1642 — the prerogative courts were not restored, and the Triennial Act remained. The monarchy was restored, but the constitutional changes Parliament had fought for were largely preserved. The Restoration was not a simple reversal of the revolution.

Key Fact

The Declaration of Breda (April 1660) promised pardon, religious toleration, army pay and land settlement — all subject to parliamentary approval. Charles returned on 29 May 1660. The Indemnity and Oblivion Act pardoned most former republicans but executed thirteen regicides.

Historians debate whether the Restoration was inevitable after Oliver Cromwell’s death. Several factors made it possible in 1660 specifically: Richard Cromwell’s failure removed the only obvious republican successor; army factionalism discredited military rule; Monck’s march provided order without demanding a particular settlement; and Charles II’s deliberate moderation in the Declaration of Breda reassured those who feared Royalist revenge. The majority of the political nation had not wanted a republic in the first place — the regicide had been achieved by a minority — and by 1660 exhaustion with military rule had created broad (if not deep) support for the King’s return.
exam_tip_html: Questions on the Restoration often ask either why the republic ended or why restoration was possible in 1660. Make sure you address both the negative (collapse of republican alternatives — Richard Cromwell, army factionalism) and the positive (Declaration of Breda’s reassurances, Monck’s role, general exhaustion). Explain the Declaration of Breda’s four promises accurately — examiners reward students who know its specific content and that all promises were deferred to Parliament.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Richard Cromwell resigned in May 1659 after eight months; General George Monck marched south from Scotland in January 1660, restored order, and enabled free elections.
  • The Declaration of Breda (April 1660) promised pardon, religious toleration, army pay and land settlement — all referred to Parliament — reassuring the political nation.
  • Charles II entered London on 29 May 1660; the Indemnity and Oblivion Act pardoned most but executed thirteen regicides; constitutional gains from the civil war period were largely retained.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Declaration of Breda issued by Charles II in April 1660.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: One accurate feature with supporting detail. Example: The Declaration of Breda promised a general pardon to all except those Parliament specifically excluded, referring the final decision on who would be excepted to Parliament rather than deciding it unilaterally.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of George Monck's role in the Restoration of 1660.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per feature. Feature 1: Monck marched south from Scotland with his well-disciplined army in January 1660, stabilising a period of constitutional chaos without declaring openly for the King. Feature 2: Monck ordered the readmission of the members excluded by Pride's Purge in 1648, allowing the Long Parliament to dissolve itself and call the Convention Parliament.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the republic collapsed between 1658 and 1660.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains multiple causes (Oliver Cromwell's death removed only unifying figure, Richard's lack of authority, army factionalism, constitutional instability of 1659, public exhaustion with military rule) linked together. Secure: Two causes developed. Developing: One cause. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: The Declaration of Breda was the most important reason for the Restoration in 1660. How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Weighs Declaration of Breda (reassuring content, deferred to Parliament) against Monck's military role (provided the mechanism), Richard Cromwell's failure (removed alternative), and general exhaustion with military rule (created the need). Reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Considers multiple factors. Developing: Mainly focuses on one factor. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Richard Cromwell was unable to maintain power as Lord Protector in 1658–1659.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three or more reasons (no military reputation, army hostility, Parliament's challenge to army role, lack of father's personal authority, inability to manage army-Parliament tensions). Linked argument. Secure: Two reasons. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Charles II's restoration in 1660 did not simply reverse all the changes made since 1642.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that prerogative courts were not restored, Triennial Act remained, Parliament retained rights confirmed 1641; Restoration was a negotiated settlement, not unconditional return; Indemnity Act acknowledged the past had to be buried not reversed. Secure: Two reasons. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Simple.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did Richard Cromwell fail as Lord Protector?
flashcard_questions.a: He had no military standing, no independent power base, and the army forced him out

flashcard_questions.a: Ordered readmission of members excluded by Pride's Purge, allowing the Long Parliament to dissolve itself
Parliament elected April 1660 that voted to restore the monarchy; summoned without royal writ

flashcard_questions.a: Pardon; religious toleration; army pay; land disputes — all referred to Parliament

What was the Indemnity and Oblivion Act?
flashcard_questions.a: 1660 Act pardoning most republicans; 13 regicides were excepted and executed

flashcard_questions.q: Were prerogative courts (Star Chamber) restored in 1660?
flashcard_questions.a: No — they were not restored; constitutional gains from the 1640s were largely kept

glossary_terms.definition: Son of Oliver Cromwell, briefly Lord Protector September 1658 to May 1659, lacking military standing and forced to resign under army pressure.
General commanding the English army in Scotland; marched south in January 1660 with his disciplined force, restoring constitutional order and making the Restoration possible.

Parliament elected in April 1660 that did not formally restore the monarchy by statute but proclaimed Charles II king, meeting before any law existed authorising it; technically a new Parliament summoned without royal writ.
Charles II's April 1660 declaration from exile in Breda, making four promises: pardon, religious toleration, settlement of army pay, and land disputes — all referred to Parliament.
An Act of Parliament passed in 1660 offering pardon for actions committed during the Civil War, but with exceptions; also requiring people to forget and not raise past grievances.

hero_image_caption: Charles II returned to England in May 1660, ending a decade of republican government.
